title: Hamas Agrees to Phased Disarmament Under Trump's Gaza Plan, but Israel Remains Skeptical
excerpt: The Board of Peace-brokered deal would see all armed groups in Gaza surrender weapons over 200-320 days, but Hamas insists Israel must first withdraw to ceasefire lines while Israeli officials reject the framework.
body:
• Trump announced a "historic agreement" for the complete disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza, brokered by his Board of Peace through talks in Cairo with Egyptian, Qatari, and Turkish mediators.
  • Hamas confirmed it agreed to surrender weapons to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, but only after Israel withdraws to October ceasefire lines, ends attacks, and allows humanitarian aid.
  • Israel rejected the framework before Trump's announcement, calling the 15-point document inadequate and demanding full demilitarisation as a precondition — setting up a standoff that could stall implementation.
  • The agreement comes amid an ongoing US-Iran military confrontation that has damaged at least 20 American bases across eight Gulf countries and driven Pentagon war costs past $29 billion.

US President Donald Trump announced on Thursday what he called a "historic agreement" for the complete disarmament of Hamas and all armed factions in Gaza — a claim that was immediately complicated by Israeli objections and Hamas preconditions that could take months to resolve.

"Today, the Board of Peace reached a HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "This is a monumental step toward lasting PEACE and SECURITY."

The deal, brokered during talks in Cairo between Hamas leaders and mediators from Egypt, Qatar and Turkey, would see armed groups hand over weapons in phases to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), a technocratic body set up to govern the enclave. A Board of Peace official estimated the disarmament process would take 200 to 320 days.

A Fragile Framework, Not a Done Deal

Within hours of Trump's announcement, the gap between rhetoric and reality became clear. Senior Hamas official Ghazi Hamad confirmed to Reuters that the group had reached an agreement but described it as a "comprehensive framework" contingent on Israel first meeting its obligations under the October 2025 ceasefire.

"We will not begin any weapons-related steps until Israel implements these commitments. Frankly, if Israel does not implement them, we will not proceed."

— Ghazi Hamad, Hamas negotiating team member

Hamas demands are specific: Israel must cease fire, stop targeted killings in Gaza, withdraw its forces to the Yellow Line demarcation established under the October agreement, and allow a surge of humanitarian aid into the enclave. The Yellow Line originally placed roughly 53% of Gaza under Israeli control, but Israel has steadily expanded that territory, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stating his intent to extend military occupation to 70% of the strip.

Israel, for its part, rejected the framework even before Trump made his announcement. An Israeli official told Reuters the country demands "the complete disarmament of Hamas, including the removal of weapons from Gaza and the complete demilitarization of the Strip as a precondition for any process." The official said the 15-point document under discussion "does not provide a satisfactory response to these demands."

Israeli settlements minister Orit Strouk of the Religious Zionist party went further, writing on Facebook: "This is a negotiation conducted over our heads, in complete contradiction to our position."

The Palestinian Islamic Jihad Movement, another armed faction in Gaza that was party to the October ceasefire, called reports of the agreement "inaccurate."

The Broader Middle East Tinderbox

The Gaza disarmament push unfolds against a volatile regional backdrop. The United States has been conducting sustained airstrikes against Iran since July 7, following Iranian attacks on three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. The strikes have hit dozens of Iranian military targets across multiple provinces, killing at least 28 IRGC personnel, according to human rights monitors, while four American servicemembers have been killed.

Iran's retaliatory strikes have damaged at least 20 US military sites across eight countries — including bases in Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Iraq, and Qatar — with satellite imagery revealing damage to advanced air defence systems, surveillance aircraft, and THAAD missile batteries. The Pentagon has estimated total war costs at $29 billion, though sources told CNN the real figure could reach $40-50 billion when including base repairs.

Iranian strikes also knocked out a sixth of Qatar's LNG export capacity — worth $20 billion annually — with QatarEnergy's CEO saying repairs would take three to five years. The economic ripple effects have sent Brent crude above $110 a barrel and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

A fragile pause in US air operations since late July has coincided with diplomatic efforts through Omani and Pakistani-Qatari channels, though neither Washington nor Tehran has committed to formal ceasefire terms.

Millions of Indians Caught in the Crossfire

For the estimated 8.5 million Indians living across the Gulf states, the dual crises in Gaza and the wider Iran conflict represent an immediate and personal threat. Indian communities in the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain, and Qatar — countries that have sustained Iranian strikes on military installations — face disrupted daily life, rising living costs driven by energy price spikes, and an uncertain security environment.

India's external affairs ministry has maintained travel advisories for the region, and the Indian embassy in Kuwait issued updated safety guidance after Iranian strikes hit multiple facilities in the country. Indian workers in Qatar's energy sector face particular uncertainty given the damage to LNG infrastructure.

What Comes Next

US officials acknowledged the path ahead is complex. "I think over the next couple weeks we'll continue to refine the details of everything, and I think we can see progress in the next month or two," a US official told CNN.

The agreement envisions phased implementation: as armed groups disarm, Israeli forces would withdraw and an International Stabilization Force, working alongside a new Palestinian police force, would assume security responsibilities. Detailed conditions are expected to be published within two weeks, with movement between phases occurring only after "verified completion of the previous" stage.

"This isn't really a trust deal. It's a conditions-based deal."

— US official involved in negotiations

But with Israel rejecting the framework's terms, Hamas insisting on Israeli compliance first, and an active US-Iran military conflict threatening to destabilise the entire region, the gap between Trump's declared breakthrough and lasting peace on the ground remains substantial. The ceasefire in Gaza has already been repeatedly violated since October, with over 1,200 Palestinians — mostly civilians — and four Israeli soldiers killed during the truce period, according to Gaza health officials and Israeli authorities.
